beats.say: Your dog is staring at you right now. That stare is changing your brain chemistry. And the dog's.
Your cat, meanwhile, knows its own name. It's just choosing not to answer.
And your horse may remember the face you pulled at it this morning.
I'm Meatball. I narrate nature. Nature, frankly, keeps trying to eat me. Today: do animals know they're pets?
Checkpoint one. True or false? When your dog gazes into your eyes, both of your brains release a love hormone.
beats.short_title: Your Dog's Stare Changes Your Brain Chemistry 🐶
beats.bonus: In the same study, long gazes raised oxytocin in both dog and owner; short glances didn't.

beats.say: True. In 2015, scientists in Japan measured oxytocin, the bonding hormone, in dogs and their owners before and after they looked at each other.
Long gazes raised it in the owners. Then it went up in the dogs too. A loop. The same loop that bonds human parents and babies.
So that thing where your dog stares at you while you eat a sandwich? That's not love. Well. It's partly love.
It's mostly the sandwich.
Now, the twist. The team tested wolves too. Hand-raised wolves that knew their keepers well. Their stares didn't start the loop.
Remember the wolves from the history of dogs episode? Same family tree. The one that moved to the suburbs learned to stare. The one in the woods did not.
To be fair, that was a small study, and some scientists say it can't prove dogs are unique. But the dog side of the loop has been measured. Your dog's stare really does something to you.
So dogs bond by looking. But do they understand what they're looking at? In Vienna, researchers trained dogs on photos of human faces, happy or angry.
And they only ever showed each dog half a face. The top half, or the bottom half.
Then they showed the other half. The dogs could still pick the happy face from the angry one. They'd learned the emotion, not just the picture.
Which means your dog knows that face you make when it eats your shoe. And has decided to eat the shoe anyway.
beats.text:
IT KNOWS.
IT ATE THE
SHOE ANYWAY.

beats.say: The dogs also learned the angry faces more slowly. The researchers think angry faces just felt unpleasant to them. Relatable.
Dogs also know when you're watching. In 2003, researchers in Germany told dogs not to touch some food, then sometimes looked away, closed their eyes, or left.
When the person kept watching, the dogs took less food. When the person stopped watching, the food went. Fast.
So your dog isn't just obeying you. It's checking whether you can see it.
beats.text:
IT'S CHECKING
IF YOU CAN
SEE IT

beats.say: And when you're not there, you're still there. In Atlanta, dogs were trained to lie still in an M R I scanner, awake, and sniff different smells.
The reward part of their brain lit up most for the smell of a familiar person. More than strangers. More than familiar dogs.
Your dog's brain has a favorite smell, and it's you. Even after you skipped the shower.
Okay. Do dogs know they're pets? They don't have a word for pet. But in 1998, Hungarian scientists ran a test built for human babies.
Owner leaves the room. Stranger comes in. Owner comes back. Babies, and dogs, behave the same way. Upset when you go. Relieved when you're back.
So to a dog, you're not an owner. You're closer to a parent. A parent who's extremely bad at fetch.
Threat check, while we're here. Dogs are friendly, loyal, and they eat anything round that falls off a plate.
Now, cats. Everyone says cats don't care. Let's test that.
Checkpoint two. True or false? Cats don't recognize their own names.
beats.quiz:
CATS DON'T
KNOW THEIR
OWN NAMES
beats.short_title: Your Cat Knows Its Name. It's Just Ignoring You 🐈
beats.bonus: It worked even when a stranger said the name.

beats.say: False. In 2019, a team in Tokyo played cats a list of words, then the cat's own name. The cats got bored of the words. Then the name came, and their ears turned.
It even worked when a stranger said it. So your cat knows its name. It's just weighing its options.
The scientist behind it thinks cats learned that their name means food, or attention. Not that it's their identity. Honestly, same. My name means dinner.
And do cats bond? In 2019, researchers in Oregon used that same baby test on cats. About two in three were securely attached to their person.
That's about the same as human babies. And a bit more than dogs, at about fifty-eight percent. Nobody tell the dogs.
Horses next. Big animals, big eyes, and apparently, very good at reading people.
Checkpoint three. True or false? Horses can tell a happy human face from an angry one.
beats.quiz:
HORSES CAN READ
HAPPY vs ANGRY
FACES
beats.short_title: Horses Can Read Your Face, and Remember It 🐴
beats.bonus: The horses were shown photos only, with no training beforehand.

beats.say: True. In 2016, horses in England were shown photos of angry and happy faces. With the angry ones, their heart rate went up.
Then in 2018, horses saw a photo of a person looking angry or happy. Hours later, they met that real person, now looking calm. And they still treated them differently.
Coo. Technically, one part of the 2016 study, which eye the horses looked with, was challenged by another scientist. The heart rate part stands.
So, horses remember your bad mood. For hours. Be nice to the horse.
Also, horses eat grass. Only grass. Horses are my friends.
And then there's the parrot that talked back. Alex, an African grey, worked with scientist Irene Pepperberg for about thirty years.
beats.chapter: The parrot who said I love you

beats.say: He learned names for about fifty objects, seven colors, and five shapes, and he could count to six.
Then one day he was shown an empty tray, and asked how many. He said: none. Something close to the idea of zero. From a bird.
Alex died in 2007. His last words to Pepperberg, the night before, were reported as: you be good. I love you.
Did Alex know he was a pet? He wasn't one, exactly. He was a colleague. But he knew exactly who she was.
One last test. And this one's about you.
Checkpoint four. True or false? Your dog's long-term stress level can match yours.
beats.quiz:
YOUR DOG'S STRESS
CAN MATCH
YOURS
beats.short_title: Your Dog's Stress Level Can Match Yours 🐕
beats.bonus: Owner personality mattered more than the dog's own personality.

beats.say: True. In 2019, scientists in Sweden measured a stress hormone in the hair of fifty-eight dogs and their owners, which records months, not minutes.
Stressed owners tended to have stressed dogs. Calm owners, calm dogs. And it wasn't about how much exercise the dog got.
Scientists can't say yet exactly why. But it seems your dog doesn't just read your face. It reads your whole month.
So. Do animals know they're pets? Probably not the word. There's no evidence a dog thinks, I am a pet.
But they know your face. Your voice. The name you gave them. When you leave, and when you come back. They know you're theirs.
And they definitely know who has the food.
For the record, the official list of animals that eat meatballs grew today. Dogs. Cats. Horses, no. Horses are my friends.
